```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center")
```

### Introduction

This project examines the differences in educational development around the world. The quality of education among a country's population is a solid indicator of the wellbeing and future advancement of a country, yet it varies significantly across different places and groups of people.

I was curious about the extent of these differences, so I turned to the data to find out. I used data from the United Nations' Human Development Reports by the UN Development Program on the educational attributes of countries' adults 25 and older, specifically 34 years (1990 to 2023) of it from the [UNDP's open database](https://hdr.undp.org/data-center/documentation-and-downloads). Note that the variables that I'm interested in were missing data past 2023 so the past couple of years (2024 and 2025) aren't included in my analysis.

I'll focus on the following main measures of educational development: the average amount of formal education attained by men and women (individually) within a country, the percentage of men and women (individually) with at least secondary education within a country, and the average amount of education attained by adults within a country. Note that secondary education, under the [UN's International Standard Classification of Education (ISCED)](https://www.uis.unesco.org/en/methods-and-tools/isced), is defined as an intermediate phase of education spanning ages 11 to 18. The dataset also includes global versions of these measures.

```{r include = FALSE}
# Loading packages
library(readxl)
library(tidyverse)
library(countrycode)
library(janitor)
library(scales)
library(patchwork)
library(gt)
library(gtExtras)
library(sf)
library(rnaturalearth)

# Preparing the data
data <- read_excel("hdr-data.xlsx") %>%
  select(-c(yearStr, value, indexCode, index, dimension, note)) %>%
  filter(!(indicatorCode %in% c("gnipc", "ineq_edu", "hdi_rank"))) %>%
  mutate((across(c(year, actualValue), as.numeric)),
         continent = countrycode(countryIsoCode,
                                 origin = "iso3c",
                                 destination = "continent"),
         # NRO is for Naoero, a country in Oceania
         # ZZK.WORLD means the global value
         continent = ifelse(countryIsoCode == "NRO", "Oceania", continent),
         # Cleaning up a country name
         country = ifelse(country == "Congo (Democratic Republic of the)",
                          "Democratic Republic of the Congo", country))

# Checking for missing values
colSums(is.na(data))
# 218 NAs in "continent", but these are just world values instead
unique(data[is.na(data$continent), ]$countryIsoCode) # ZZK.WORLD

# Checking for duplicate rows
anyDuplicated(data) # 0

# Checking for duplicate (year, country, continent, indicator) combinations because there should
# only be one indicator per country per year
get_dupes(data, year, country, continent, indicator) # no duplicate combinations found
```

Just as a preliminary look, in this initial plot of the average amount of education worldwide in years, it's clear that the world is gradually becoming more educated as a whole:

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
# Graphing the global education mean over time
data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode == "mys",
         is.na(continent)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = actualValue)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = ~ paste(.x, "Years"),
                     limits = c(0, 9)) +
  labs(x = "", y = "",
       title = "Mean Amount of Education of Adults* Worldwide (1990-2023)",
       caption = "*Adults 25+") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.title.y = element_text(margin = margin(t = 0, r = 15, b = 0, l = 0)),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 14))
```

```{r echo=FALSE}
# Getting the MYS in 1990 and 2023
mys_1990 <- pull(filter(data, indicatorCode == "mys", is.na(continent), year == 1990), actualValue)
mys_2023 <- pull(filter(data, indicatorCode == "mys", is.na(continent), year == 2023), actualValue)
```

The world's average education amount has been steadily growing for the past 3 decades from \~`r round(mys_1990, 0)` years in 1990 to \~`r round(mys_2023, 0)` years in 2023 (a change of \~`r round(mys_2023 - mys_1990, 0)` years!). In fact, it has grown every single year, at a rate of \~`r round((mys_2023 - mys_1990) / (2023 - 1990), 1)` years per year, or 1 year per decade.

However, if we look into how the level of education varies by gender and geographically, some disparities do emerge...

### Gender inequality

To view educational inequalities in terms of gender, I'm using two metrics: (1) the average amount of formal education attained by each gender, and (2) the percentage of adults in each gender who have at least some level of secondary education.

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
# Graphing the global education mean by gender over time
p1 <- data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode %in% c("mys_f", "mys_m"),
         is.na(continent)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = actualValue, colour = indicatorCode)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("mys_m" = "#4a72b8", "mys_f" = "#f8766d"),
                    labels = c("mys_m" = "Males", "mys_f" = "Females")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = ~ paste(.x, "Years"),
                     limits = c(0, 10)) +
  labs(x = "", y = "", colour = "",
       title = "Mean Amount of Education of Adults*") +
  guides(color = guide_legend(reverse = TRUE)) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.title.y = element_text(margin = margin(t = 0, r = 15, b = 0, l = 0)),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 12),
        legend.position = c(0.15, 0.9))

# Graphing the percentage of people who have secondary education by gender over time
p2 <- data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode %in% c("se_f", "se_m"),
         is.na(continent)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = actualValue, fill = indicatorCode)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("se_m" = "#4a72b8", "se_f" = "#f8766d"),
                    labels = c("se_m" = "Males", "se_f" = "Females")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent(scale = 1),
                     limits = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(x = "", y = "", fill = "",
       title = "Percent of Adults* With Secondary Education") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.title.y = element_text(margin = margin(t = 0, r = 15, b = 0, l = 0)),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 12),
        legend.position = c(0.15, 0.9)) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(reverse = TRUE))

(p1 | p2) + plot_annotation(title = "Gender Inequality in Education Worldwide (1990-2023)",
                            theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 14, hjust = 0.5)),
                            caption = "*Adults 25+")
```

```{r include=FALSE}
# Creating a wider data frame with indicators as separate columns
wider_data <- data %>%
  group_by(year, country, continent, countryIsoCode, indicatorCode) %>%
  summarize(actualValue = mean(actualValue, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = indicatorCode, values_from = actualValue) %>%
  # Getting the yearly gender gaps
  mutate(gap_mys = mys_m - mys_f,
         gap_se = se_m - se_f)
```

For both metrics, the amount of education for females has never been more than for males: although they've been increasing at similar speeds --- the lines in both charts are nearly parallel --- there has always been a gap of around one year or ~`r round(mean(filter(wider_data, is.na(continent))$gap_se), 0)` percentage points between them.

Despite this, that gap has been shrinking for the past few years. In 2020, the magnitude of the gap dropped to a new low of ~`r round(filter(wider_data, is.na(continent), year == 2020)$gap_mys, 1)` years, to ~`r round(filter(wider_data, is.na(continent), year == 2021)$gap_mys, 1)` years in 2021 and 2022, and ~`r round(filter(wider_data, is.na(continent), year == 2023)$gap_mys, 1)` years in 2023. Similarly, the percentage of males vs. females with secondary education worldwide has shrunk to ~`r round(filter(wider_data, is.na(continent), year == 2023)$gap_se, 0)` percentage points in 2023.

So where specifically in the world do the highest gender gaps consistently occur?

To answer this question, I found the countries that ranked in the highest 10 countries at least once during the 34-year period, in terms of the gender gap for both metrics simultaneously, then I calculated the average gender gaps for each metric as a simple subtraction such that a positive gender difference mean that males had higher values.

```{r echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
# Getting the countries with the largest gender gaps
high_gender_gap <- wider_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(continent)) %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  mutate(rank_mys = rank(desc(gap_mys), ties.method = "min"),
         rank_se = rank(desc(gap_se), ties.method = "min")) %>%
  filter(rank_mys <= 10 & rank_se <= 10) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(continent, country) %>%
  summarize(times_in_top_10 = n(),
            mean_gap_mys = mean(gap_mys, na.rm = TRUE),
            mean_gap_se = mean(gap_se, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop")

# Creating a table of the countries with consistently high gender gaps
high_gender_gap %>%
  select(-c(mean_gap_mys, mean_gap_se)) %>%
  arrange(desc(times_in_top_10)) %>%
  gt() %>%
  cols_label(continent = "Continent",
             country = "Country",
             times_in_top_10 = "# of Times in Highest 10") %>%
  cols_align("center") %>%
  tab_header(title = "Countries With Consistently High Gender Gaps* (1990-2023)") %>%
  tab_style(style = cell_text(size = px(18)),
            locations = cells_title(groups = "title")) %>%
  tab_style(style = cell_text(v_align = "middle"),
            locations = cells_column_labels(columns = everything())) %>%
  tab_options(table.border.top.color = "white",
              table.border.bottom.color = "grey60",
              heading.border.bottom.color = "grey60",
              column_labels.border.top.color = "grey60",
              column_labels.border.bottom.color = "grey60",
              table_body.hlines.color = "white",
              table_body.border.bottom.color = "grey60") %>%
  opt_row_striping(row_striping = TRUE) %>%
  tab_source_note(source_note = "*Ranked in terms of both the average amount of education and the percentage with secondary education (in each gender for people over 25) simultaneously.")
```

There are `r nrow(high_gender_gap)` countries in this table (there are `r n_distinct(data$countryIsoCode)` countries in the data in total), of which the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Liberia have been there in every year of the 34. The only continents in this table are Africa and Asia:

```{r echo=FALSE}
high_gender_gap %>%
  group_by(continent) %>%
  summarize(n = n(),
            pct = round(n/340 * 100, 2)) %>%  # 340 because 34 years * highest 10
  arrange(desc(pct)) %>%
  gt() %>%
  cols_align("center") %>%
  cols_label(continent = "Continent",
             n = "# of Times in Highest 10",
             pct = "% of Countries") %>%
  tab_header(title = "Continents With Consistently High Gender Gaps* (1990-2023)") %>%
  tab_style(style = cell_text(size = px(18)),
            locations = cells_title(groups = "title")) %>%
  tab_options(table.border.top.color = "white",
              table.border.bottom.color = "grey60",
              heading.border.bottom.color = "grey60",
              column_labels.border.top.color = "grey60",
              column_labels.border.bottom.color = "grey60",
              table_body.hlines.color = "white",
              table_body.border.bottom.color = "grey60") %>%
  opt_row_striping(row_striping = TRUE) %>%
  tab_source_note(source_note = "*Ranked in terms of both the average amount of education and the percentage with secondary education (in each gender for people over 25) simultaneously.")
```

So how large have these gender gaps been recently? For this part, I'm choosing to zero in on 2023 because that's the last year in the data.

### Geographic inequality

This section analyzes the geographic variation in terms of the average amount of education for adults, as a composite measure, to contrast across individual continents and countries.

As an initial look, here's a graph of each continent's average amount of education:

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=5}
# Graphing the global education mean by continent over time
data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode == "mys", !is.na(continent)) %>%
  group_by(continent, year) %>%
  summarise(mean_mys = mean(actualValue, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(continent = factor(continent,
                            levels = c("Europe", "Oceania", "Americas", "Asia", "Africa"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_mys, colour = continent)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "", y = "",
       title = "Average Amount of Education of Adults* by Continent (1990-2023)",
       colour = "Continent",
       caption = "*Adults 25+") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = ~ paste(.x, "Years")) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.title.y = element_text(margin = margin(t = 0, r = 15, b = 0, l = 0)),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 14)) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Set2")
```

From this graph, we see that the absolute rankings have been the same since 1990 and that every continent except for Oceania has grown at a similar rate. In 2023, Oceania, the Americas, and Asia were all at similar places (all around an 8-year average) while Europe remained higher than these three continents by ~4 years, and Africa remained lower than these three continents by ~4 years too. This is still encouraging --- despite the fact that the absolute rankings haven't changed, the main trend has been steady growth across all continents throughout the past few decades.
```{r echo=FALSE}
# Putting the yearly gaps in a table
data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode == "mys", !is.na(continent)) %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(Highest = country[which.max(actualValue)],
            Lowest = country[which.min(actualValue)],
            Gap = round(max(actualValue, na.rm = TRUE) - min(actualValue, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  gt() %>%
  cols_align("center") %>%
  cols_label(year = "Year") %>%
  tab_header(title = "Gaps in Education Across Countries Over Time") %>%
  tab_style(style = cell_text(size = px(18)),
            locations = cells_title(groups = "title")) %>%
  tab_options(table.border.top.color = "white",
              table.border.bottom.color = "grey60",
              heading.border.bottom.color = "grey60",
              column_labels.border.top.color = "grey60",
              column_labels.border.bottom.color = "grey60",
              table_body.hlines.color = "white",
              table_body.border.bottom.color = "grey60") %>%
  opt_row_striping(row_striping = TRUE)
```

Again, I want to know which countries have the most consistently low averages, so here are the countries that have been in the bottom 10 at least once, in terms of the average amount of education of its population over 25 years. (Note that the tie-breaking method included all countries of the same rank if there was a tie.)

```{r echo=FALSE}
# Making a table of the least educated countries in terms of the mean (1990-2023)
bottom_countries <- data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode == "mys") %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  mutate(rank = rank(actualValue, ties.method = "min")) %>%
  filter(rank <= 10) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  count(continent, country, name = "times_in_bottom_10")

# Making a table of the countries with consistently low education rates
bottom_countries %>%
  arrange(desc(times_in_bottom_10)) %>%
  gt() %>%
  cols_align("center") %>%
  cols_label(continent = "Continent",
             country = "Country",
             times_in_bottom_10 = "# of Times in Bottom 10") %>%
  tab_header(title = "Countries With Consistently Low Education Rates (1990-2023)") %>%
  tab_style(style = cell_text(size = px(18)),
            locations = cells_title(groups = "title")) %>%
  tab_options(table.border.top.color = "white",
              table.border.bottom.color = "grey60",
              heading.border.bottom.color = "grey60",
              column_labels.border.top.color = "grey60",
              column_labels.border.bottom.color = "grey60",
              table_body.hlines.color = "white",
              table_body.border.bottom.color = "grey60") %>%
  opt_row_striping(row_striping = TRUE)
```

There are 17 countries that have been in the bottom 10 at least once, of which 4 countries (Afghanistan, Guinea, Mali, and Niger) have been there in every year of the 34. And again, the only continents in this table are Africa, which appears 14 times, and Asia, which appears 3 times:

```{r echo=FALSE}
bottom_countries %>%
  group_by(continent) %>%
  summarize(n = n(),
            pct = round(n/340 * 100, 2)) %>%  # 340 because 34 years * bottom 10
  arrange(desc(pct)) %>%
  gt() %>%
  cols_align("center") %>%
  cols_label(continent = "Continent",
             n = "# of Times in Bottom 10",
             pct = "% of Countries") %>%
  tab_header(title = "Continents With Consistently Low Education Rates (1990-2023)") %>%
  tab_style(style = cell_text(size = px(18)),
            locations = cells_title(groups = "title")) %>%
  tab_options(table.border.top.color = "white",
              table.border.bottom.color = "grey60",
              heading.border.bottom.color = "grey60",
              column_labels.border.top.color = "grey60",
              column_labels.border.bottom.color = "grey60",
              table_body.hlines.color = "white",
              table_body.border.bottom.color = "grey60") %>%
  opt_row_striping(row_striping = TRUE)
```

```{r include=FALSE}
# Getting the countries with consistently high education rates
top_countries <- data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode == "mys",
         !is.na(continent)) %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  # Ranking countries by the metric in ascending order
  mutate(rank = rank(actualValue, ties.method = "min")) %>%
  # Keeping only the top 10 for each year
  filter(rank >= 10) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  # Counting how many times each country appeared in the top 10
  count(continent, country, name = "times_in_top_10")

# Making a table of the frequency of appearance in the top 10
freq_top_countries <- top_countries %>%
  group_by(times_in_top_10) %>%
  summarize(freq = n())

# The highest ranked countries are consistently highly ranked, where `r pull(filter(freq_top_countries, times_in_top_10 == 34), freq)` countries appeared in all 34 years. 
```
